claim: Eco-HAB is an open source, RFID-based system for automated measurement and analysis of social preference and in-cohort sociability in mice.
source: Eco-HAB is an open source, RFID-based system for automated measurement and analysis of social preference and in-cohort sociability in mice.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the system.

claim: Eco-HAB requires no contact between a human experimenter and tested animals.
source: It requires no contact between a human experimenter and tested animals, overcoming the confounding factors that lead to irreproducible assessment of murine social behavior between laboratories.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the system in the abstract.

claim: Eco-HAB overcomes confounding factors that lead to irreproducible assessment of murine social behavior between laboratories.
source: It requires no contact between a human experimenter and tested animals, overcoming the confounding factors that lead to irreproducible assessment of murine social behavior between laboratories.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the system in the abstract.

claim: In Eco-HAB, group-housed animals live in a spacious, four-compartment apparatus with shadowed areas and narrow tunnels, resembling natural burrows.
source: In Eco-HAB, group-housed animals live in a spacious, four-compartment apparatus with shadowed areas and narrow tunnels, resembling natural burrows.
evidence: This describes the physical design of the apparatus.

claim: Eco-HAB allows for assessment of the tendency of mice to voluntarily spend time together in ethologically relevant mouse group sizes.
source: Eco-HAB allows for assessment of the tendency of mice to voluntarily spend time together in ethologically relevant mouse group sizes.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the system in the abstract.

claim: The developed protocols and standardized behavioral measures in Eco-HAB demonstrate high replicability.
source: The developed protocols and standardized behavioral measures demonstrate high replicability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by reproducibility data shown in Figures 5-8.

claim: Unlike classic three-chambered sociability tests, Eco-HAB provides measurements of spontaneous, ecologically relevant social behaviors in group-housed animals.
source: Unlike classic three-chambered sociability tests, Eco-HAB provides measurements of spontaneous, ecologically relevant social behaviors in group-housed animals.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to existing methods in the abstract.

claim: Results from Eco-HAB are obtained faster, with less manpower, and without confounding factors compared to manual testing.
source: Results are obtained faster, with less manpower, and without confounding factors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Conventional tests of social phenotyping have repeatedly proven inefficient in differentiating certain genotypes and replicating these differences across laboratories and protocol conditions.
source: Conventional tests of social phenotyping have repeatedly proven inefficient in differentiating certain genotypes and replicating these differences across laboratories and protocol conditions (Chadman et al., 2008; Moy et al., 2004; Pearson et al., 2010; Tabuchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In humans, anxiety and susceptibility to stress are co-morbid to autism spectrum disorders.
source: For example, in most studies of autism and sociability in mice, behavioral effects related to anxiety and susceptibility to stress have been overlooked, even though, in humans, both these factors are co-morbid to autism spectrum disorders (Simonoff et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simonoff et al., 2008.

claim: Anxiety is the most common cause of social impairments in humans.
source: In fact, anxiety is the most common cause of social impairments in humans.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the introduction.

claim: Some people with ASD never develop so-called 'associated' anxiety.
source: Since some people with ASD never develop so-called 'associated' anxiety, we can assume that underlying neural mechanisms are at least partially different.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the introduction.

claim: The three-chambered apparatus social approach test (3ChA) is a commonly used method for assessing social interactions of rodents.
source: Social interactions of rodents are often assessed using the three-chambered apparatus social approach test (3ChA), in which lone mice are given the choice between approaching a caged conspecific or an inanimate object.
evidence: This describes a standard method in the field.

claim: The popularity of 3ChA stems from its simplicity, inexpensive cage construction, and the lack of alternative tests.
source: The popularity of 3ChA stems from its simplicity, inexpensive cage construction, and the lack of alternative tests.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the test's widespread use.

claim: The 3ChA test has poor cross-laboratory standardization and reproducibility.
source: However, its poor cross-laboratory standardization and reproducibility call for alternative testing.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the 3ChA test.

claim: Different laboratories have come to opposite conclusions concerning sociability of the same autistic phenotype mouse model.
source: At times, different laboratories have come to opposite conclusions concerning sociability of the same autistic phenotype mouse model (Chadman et al., 2008; Tabuchi et al., 2007, p. 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Even within a single laboratory, reproducible results can be difficult to obtain in 3ChA testing.
source: Even within a single laboratory, reproducible results can be difficult to obtain (Jamain et al., 2008; El-Kordi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Irreproducibility of conventional behavioral tests across laboratories has been identified as one of the most important threats to science and its public understanding.
source: Irreproducibility of conventional behavioral tests across laboratories (Crabbe et al., 1999) has recently been identified as one of the most important threats to science and its public understanding (Nature, 2015; Morrison, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to publications discussing the reproducibility crisis.

claim: Handling by human experimenters with unique scents and variable handling abilities is a confounding factor in behavioral testing.
source: The known factors that lead to severe behavioral abnormalities in both males and females (Beery and Kaufer, 2015; Heinrichs and Koob, 2006; Sandi and Haller, 2015) and which are particularly difficult to control include: handling by human experimenters with unique scents and variable handling abilities (Chesler et al., 2002; Sorge et al., 2014), levels of animal familiarity with the experimental environment, and housing of animals in social isolation (a practice forbidden by EU ethical standards unless justified by experimental requirements).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these effects.

claim: Levels of animal familiarity with the experimental environment is a confounding factor in behavioral testing.
source: The known factors that lead to severe behavioral abnormalities in both males and females (Beery and Kaufer, 2015; Heinrichs and Koob, 2006; Sandi and Haller, 2015) and which are particularly difficult to control include: handling by human experimenters with unique scents and variable handling abilities (Chesler et al., 2002; Sorge et al., 2014), levels of animal familiarity with the experimental environment, and housing of animals in social isolation (a practice forbidden by EU ethical standards unless justified by experimental requirements).
evidence: This is stated as a known confounding factor.

claim: Housing of animals in social isolation is a confounding factor in behavioral testing.
source: The known factors that lead to severe behavioral abnormalities in both males and females (Beery and Kaufer, 2015; Heinrichs and Koob, 2006; Sandi and Haller, 2015) and which are particularly difficult to control include: handling by human experimenters with unique scents and variable handling abilities (Chesler et al., 2002; Sorge et al., 2014), levels of animal familiarity with the experimental environment, and housing of animals in social isolation (a practice forbidden by EU ethical standards unless justified by experimental requirements).
evidence: This is stated as a known confounding factor.

claim: Housing of animals in social isolation is forbidden by EU ethical standards unless justified by experimental requirements.
source: The known factors that lead to severe behavioral abnormalities in both males and females (Beery and Kaufer, 2015; Heinrichs and Koob, 2006; Sandi and Haller, 2015) and which are particularly difficult to control include: handling by human experimenters with unique scents and variable handling abilities (Chesler et al., 2002; Sorge et al., 2014), levels of animal familiarity with the experimental environment, and housing of animals in social isolation (a practice forbidden by EU ethical standards unless justified by experimental requirements).
evidence: This is stated as a regulatory requirement.

claim: Confounding factors present in published 3ChA results can be eliminated by development of automated, ethologically relevant behavioral tests.
source: These confounding factors, all present in published 3ChA results (El-Kordi et al., 2013), can be eliminated by development of automated, ethologically relevant behavioral tests, which measure spontaneous sociability in group-housed, familiar mice without the presence of a human experimenter.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for developing Eco-HAB.

claim: Irreproducibility and high manpower costs of manual testing have led to the development of automated behavioral tests.
source: Irreproducibility and high manpower costs of manual testing have led to the development of automated behavioral tests.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for automation.

claim: Automated behavioral tests allow assessment of individual behavior of group-housed rodents using either radio-frequency-based identification (RFID) or advanced video/image processing.
source: These allow assessment of individual behavior of group-housed rodents using either radio-frequency-based identification (RFID) (Galsworthy et al., 2005; Knapska et al., 2006; Voikar et al., 2010; Schaefer and Claridge-Chang, 2012; Howerton et al., 2012) or advanced video/image processing (de Chaumont et al., 2012; Pérez-Escudero et al., 2014; Shemesh et al., 2013; Weissbrod et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies using these technologies.

claim: Video-based systems have serious limitations in ethologically relevant settings containing shadowed areas and narrow corridors.
source: Video-based systems, often employed for tracking social interactions, have serious limitations in ethologically relevant settings containing shadowed areas and narrow corridors.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of video-based tracking.

claim: RFID systems are more invasive than video-tracking solutions due to the necessity of injecting animals with electronic tags.
source: Although RFID systems are more invasive than video-tracking solutions due to the necessity of injecting animals with electronic tags, high intra- and inter-laboratory reliability have been confirmed (Codita et al., 2012; Krackow et al., 2010; Puścian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a trade-off of RFID technology.

claim: RFID systems have high intra- and inter-laboratory reliability.
source: Although RFID systems are more invasive than video-tracking solutions due to the necessity of injecting animals with electronic tags, high intra- and inter-laboratory reliability have been confirmed (Codita et al., 2012; Krackow et al., 2010; Puścian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies confirming reliability.

claim: Present commercial forms of RFID systems are not suitable for measuring sociability.
source: However, their present commercial form is not suitable for measuring sociability.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing RFID systems.

claim: The design of Eco-HAB was inspired by results of ethological field studies in mice.
source: This is a fully automated, open-source system based on RFID technology and inspired by the results of ethological field studies in mice (Dell'omo et al., 1998, 2000; Lopucki and Szymroszczyk, 2003; Andrzejewski, 2002; Lewejohann et al., 2004; Lopucki, 2007; Daan et al., 2011; von Merten et al., 2014; Chalfin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ethological studies.

claim: Eco-HAB reduces stress by tracking the tendency of animals to voluntarily spend time together in an environment to which they have already been accustomed.
source: Eco-HAB reduces stress by tracking the tendency of animals to voluntarily spend time together in an environment to which they have already been accustomed and utilizes novel sociability measures for group-housed mice.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the system design.

claim: Eco-HAB is equipped with software for automated data extraction and analysis, enabling quick evaluation of social activity.
source: The system is equipped with software for automated data extraction and analysis, enabling quick evaluation of social activity.
evidence: This describes a feature of the system.

claim: Eco-HAB provides results comparable to the classic three-chamber test when carried out in stress-reducing conditions for single-housed animals.
source: By comparing Eco-HAB results from several mouse models having different sociability levels, we show that this apparatus provides results comparable to the classic three-chamber test when carried out in stress-reducing conditions for single-housed animals.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the validation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Data from Eco-HAB are obtained much faster, with high reliability, less manpower, and are not confounded by factors that usually blur results of manual testing.
source: As a result of the innovative electronic solutions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) developed for Eco-HAB, data from this system are obtained much faster, with high reliability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), less manpower (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and are not confounded by the factors that usually blur results of manual testing.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the referenced figure supplements.

claim: The cost of building an Eco-HAB system suitable for testing up to 12 animals at the same time is approximately 2000 EUR.
source: The cost of building an Eco-HAB system, suitable for testing up to 12 animals at the same time (approximately 2000 EUR), is comparable to the cost of one three-chambered apparatus.
evidence: This is stated as a cost estimate for the system.

claim: The cost of building an Eco-HAB system is comparable to the cost of one three-chambered apparatus.
source: The cost of building an Eco-HAB system, suitable for testing up to 12 animals at the same time (approximately 2000 EUR), is comparable to the cost of one three-chambered apparatus.
evidence: This is stated as a cost comparison.

claim: Eco-HAB consists of four housing compartments occupying four corners of a larger square, bridged by tube-shaped corridors.
source: Eco-HAB (Figure 1 and Video 1) consists of four housing compartments, occupying four corners of a larger square, bridged by tube-shaped corridors.
evidence: This is described in text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The corridors in Eco-HAB enable mice to travel freely and select preferred areas within the available territory.
source: These corridors enable mice to travel freely and select preferred areas within the available territory.
evidence: This describes the function of the corridors.

claim: Two chambers on opposing corners of Eco-HAB offer access to food and water (ad libitum) and provide shelter and secluded places where mice can sleep and rest.
source: Two chambers on opposing corners of the square offer access to food and water (ad libitum) and provide shelter and secluded places where mice can sleep and rest.
evidence: This describes the design of two of the compartments.

claim: Two compartments in Eco-HAB have similar designs except that they contain no food or water and one of the corners is equipped with an impassable, transparent, and perforated partition behind which an olfactory stimulus may be presented.
source: The two other compartments have similar designs except that they contain no food or water and one of the corners is equipped with an impassable, transparent, and perforated partition behind which an olfactory stimulus may be presented.
evidence: This describes the design of the other two compartments.

claim: Mice in the wild have a natural tendency to live in family-based groups having many members.
source: Acknowledging the natural tendency of mice to live in family-based groups having many members (Andrzejewski, 2002), Eco-HAB is designed for testing littermate cohorts of up to 12 subjects.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an ethological study.

claim: Eco-HAB is designed for testing littermate cohorts of up to 12 subjects.
source: Acknowledging the natural tendency of mice to live in family-based groups having many members (Andrzejewski, 2002), Eco-HAB is designed for testing littermate cohorts of up to 12 subjects.
evidence: This describes the capacity of the system.

claim: Animals in Eco-HAB are tracked individually by subcutaneously injected microtransponders that emit a unique identification code when mice pass under RFID antennas.
source: Animals are tracked individually by subcutaneously injected microtransponders that emit a unique identification code when mice pass under RFID antennas placed on both ends of each corridor.
evidence: This describes the tracking method used in Eco-HAB.

claim: RFID antennas in Eco-HAB are placed on both ends of each corridor.
source: Animals are tracked individually by subcutaneously injected microtransponders that emit a unique identification code when mice pass under RFID antennas placed on both ends of each corridor.
evidence: This describes the placement of the antennas.

claim: Eco-HAB is a computer-controlled system that eliminates human handling and allows for continuous data collection lasting for days or even weeks with minimal presence of human observers.
source: As Eco-HAB is a computer-controlled system, it eliminates human handling and allows for continuous data collection lasting for days or even weeks with minimal presence of human observers.
evidence: This describes the automated nature of the system.

claim: The position of every mouse in an Eco-HAB system can be tracked.
source: Since the position of every mouse in an Eco-HAB system can be tracked, a novel in-cohort measure of sociability, based on the tendency of mice for spending time together, can be assessed.
evidence: This describes a capability of the tracking system.

claim: Both Eco-HAB measures--in-cohort sociability and scent-based social approach--allow similar conclusions about mouse behavior to be reached.
source: Notably, results show that both Eco-HAB measures--in-cohort sociability and scent-based social approach--allow similar conclusions about mouse behavior to be reached.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Scent-based social approach is equivalent to the most natural social exploratory behavior observed in wild populations of mice.
source: The latter measure is equivalent to the most natural social exploratory behavior observed in wild populations of mice.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the measure.

claim: Odor-mediated communication is crucial for survival and plays a key role in all murine social behaviors.
source: Odor-mediated communication is crucial for survival and plays a key role in all murine social behaviors: mating and reproduction, territory maintenance, development of stable inter-group hierarchy (Stockley et al., 2013), and integration of populations of mice in the wild (Andrzejewski, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mouse behavior.

claim: Mice have developed the ability to learn and remember information associated with olfactory cues as effectively as primates recall visually related cues.
source: Mice have developed the ability to learn and remember information associated with olfactory cues as effectively as primates recall visually related cues (Schellinck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on mouse olfactory learning.

claim: Unfamiliar rodents in their natural habitats tend to avoid each other and, if forced to interact openly, often become aggressive.
source: It has been shown that unfamiliar rodents in their natural habitats tend to avoid each other and, if forced to interact openly, often become aggressive (Lopucki, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an ethological study.

claim: Unfamiliar mice, irrespective of their sexes, are attracted by the scent of a conspecific rather than by its presence.
source: Unfamiliar mice, irrespective of their sexes, are attracted by the scent of a conspecific rather than by its presence (Andrzejewski, 2002; Lopucki and Szymroszczyk, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ethological studies.

claim: Scents have been previously employed in the 3ChA test.
source: For that reason, scents have been previously employed in the 3ChA test (Ryan et al., 2008) although, more commonly, unfamiliar animals are introduced into the social chamber.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study using scents in 3ChA.

claim: In the final Eco-HAB protocol, cohorts of 7 to 12 same-sex mice are subjected to 72-hr testing.
source: In the final protocol, cohorts of 7 to 12 same-sex mice are subjected to 72-hr testing.
evidence: This describes the optimized protocol.

claim: During the adaptation phase (first 48 hr) of Eco-HAB testing, mice can freely explore the whole apparatus.
source: During an adaptation phase (first 48 hr) mice can freely explore the whole apparatus.
evidence: This describes the first phase of the protocol.

claim: The odor-based social-preference testing phase in Eco-HAB starts with simultaneous introduction of two different beddings to two testing compartments.
source: The odor-based social-preference testing phase starts with simultaneous introduction of two different beddings to two testing compartments.
evidence: This describes the second phase of the protocol.

claim: In Eco-HAB testing, one bedding comes from a cage housing a mouse of the same sex, age, and strain as the tested animals ('social' scent), while the other is plain, new bedding from stock.
source: One of the beddings comes from a cage housing a mouse of the same sex, age, and strain as the tested animals ('social' scent), while the other is plain, new bedding from stock.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the testing phase.

claim: In Eco-HAB, mice are allowed to explore both stimuli for 24 hr.
source: Mice are allowed to explore both stimuli for 24 hr.
evidence: This describes the duration of the testing phase.

claim: Social approach in Eco-HAB is measured as the relative increase in time spent in the compartment containing social scent divided by the time spent in the opposite chamber that contains bedding without the social scent.
source: Social approach is measured as the relative increase in time spent in the compartment containing social scent divided by the time spent in the opposite chamber that contains bedding without the social scent.
evidence: This describes how the social approach measure is calculated.

claim: BALB/c mice showed social preference only in low-stress conditions in the 3ChA test.
source: BALB/c mice (Figure 2B) showed social preference only in low-stress conditions (n = 17), and they avoided social interactions when tested in a typical experimental setting (n = 11).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and described in the text.

claim: BALB/c mice avoided social interactions when tested in a typical experimental setting in the 3ChA test.
source: BALB/c mice (Figure 2B) showed social preference only in low-stress conditions (n = 17), and they avoided social interactions when tested in a typical experimental setting (n = 11).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and described in the text.

claim: C57BL/6 mice displayed social preference in both stressful and stress reducing conditions in the 3ChA test.
source: In contrast, C57BL/6 mice displayed social preference in both stressful (n = 11) and stress reducing (n = 38) conditions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and described in the text.

claim: In both tested strains (C57BL/6 and BALB/c), conventional experimental treatment (high stress) reduced locomotor activity in the 3ChA test.
source: In both tested strains, conventional experimental treatment (high stress) reduced locomotor activity which may have attenuated the number of social contacts and influenced their propensity for exploration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and 2E and described in the text.

claim: Valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice display increased social approach in Eco-HAB testing.
source: Automated Eco-HAB testing (Figure 3A) showed that valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice display increased social approach.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and described in the text.

claim: 3ChA testing revealed increased social approach in valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice when subjects were single-housed.
source: Interestingly, 3ChA testing revealed the same result when subjects were single-housed (Figure 3B), but no differences between VPA and control animals when subjects were group-housed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and described in the text.

claim: 3ChA testing showed no differences between VPA and control C57BL/6 animals when subjects were group-housed.
source: Interestingly, 3ChA testing revealed the same result when subjects were single-housed (Figure 3B), but no differences between VPA and control animals when subjects were group-housed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and described in the text.

claim: In BALB/c mice, only Eco-HAB revealed a significant increase in social behavior caused by VPA.
source: In BALB/c mice, despite significant attempts at reducing experimental stress in 3ChA testing, only Eco-HAB revealed a significant increase in social behavior caused by VPA (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and described in the text.

claim: Manual assessment with the use of the 3ChA showed the same trend in single-housed BALB/c animals as Eco-HAB; however, differences were blurred by a huge variability in the scores.
source: Manual assessment with the use of the 3ChA showed the same trend in single-housed animals; however, differences were blurred by a huge variability in the scores (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F and described in the text.

claim: No differences were found between VPA and control, group-housed BALB/c subjects in 3ChA testing.
source: Again, no differences were found between VPA and control, group-housed BALB/c subjects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and described in the text.

claim: VPA C57BL/6 mice stay together more often than respective controls in Eco-HAB.
source: Results show that VPA C57BL/6 mice stay together more often than respective controls (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and 3D and described in the text.

claim: VPA BALB/c mice stay together more often than respective controls in Eco-HAB.
source: The same tendency was found for VPA BALB/c animals (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and 3H and described in the text.

claim: Fmr1 knockout mice are a well-established animal model of autism.
source: These mice are a well-established animal model of autism and have repeatedly been reported to display social deficits (Bernardet and Crusio, 2006; Mines et al., 2010; Mineur et al., 2006; Santos et al., 2014; Sidhu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Fmr1 knockout mice have repeatedly been reported to display social deficits.
source: These mice are a well-established animal model of autism and have repeatedly been reported to display social deficits (Bernardet and Crusio, 2006; Mines et al., 2010; Mineur et al., 2006; Santos et al., 2014; Sidhu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Fmr1 knockouts display a lower level of social approach compared to wild-type in Eco-HAB.
source: The Fmr1 knockouts display a lower level of social approach and decreased in-cohort sociability as compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and described in the text.

claim: Fmr1 knockouts display decreased in-cohort sociability compared to wild-type in Eco-HAB.
source: The Fmr1 knockouts display a lower level of social approach and decreased in-cohort sociability as compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and described in the text.

claim: The results clearly confirm the impairment of social behavior in Fmr1 knockouts, as has been observed previously.
source: The results clearly confirm the impairment of social behavior in Fmr1 knockouts, as has been observed previously.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the Fmr1 experiments.

claim: Approach to social odor in valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice gradually decreases during first 4 hr of testing.
source: Approach to social odor in (a) valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice (n = 26) gradually decreases during first 4 hr of testing, whereas in (b) valproate-treated BALB/c mice (n = 18) it is high and stable during this time.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and described in the figure legend.

claim: Approach to social odor in valproate-treated BALB/c mice is high and stable during the first 4 hr of testing.
source: Approach to social odor in (a) valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice (n = 26) gradually decreases during first 4 hr of testing, whereas in (b) valproate-treated BALB/c mice (n = 18) it is high and stable during this time.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and described in the figure legend.

claim: In control C57BL/6 mice and BALB/c mice, approach to social odor gradually decreases with a faster decrease rate in C57BL/6 mice.
source: In control C57BL/6 mice (n = 35) and BALB/c mice (n = 20) approach to social odor gradually decreases with a faster decrease rate in C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and described in the figure legend.

claim: The dynamics of response to social stimuli may differ depending on the tested strain of mice.
source: Importantly, data collected in Eco-HAB show that the dynamics of response to social stimuli may differ depending on the tested strain of mice (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both standardized Eco-HAB measures, approach to social odor and in-cohort sociability, were highly reproducible in two independent studies of Fmr1 knockout animals.
source: Results confirm social impairments of Fmr1 knockouts and show that both standardized Eco-HAB measures, approach to social odor (Figure 6) and in-cohort sociability (Figure 7) were highly reproducible in those two independent studies.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6 and 7 and described in the text.

claim: Within-subject comparison reveals high reproducibility of sociability assessment in particular subjects over time in Eco-HAB.
source: Within-subject comparison (Figure 8) reveals high reproducibility of sociability assessment in particular subjects over time.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 and described in the text.

claim: Eco-HAB is a reliable tool that is reproducible for a number of tasks, from assessment of individual sociability, through phenotyping of subsequent cohorts of mice, to cross-laboratory comparisons.
source: Taken together, these studies show that Eco-HAB is a reliable tool that is reproducible for a number of tasks, from assessment of individual sociability, through phenotyping of subsequent cohorts of mice, to cross-laboratory comparisons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the reproducibility experiments.

claim: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in control C57BL/6 mice in Eco-HAB.
source: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in either of the tested groups: (a) control (n = 23) or (b) valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice (n = 26), (c) control (n = 32) or (d) valproate-treated BALB/c mice (n = 19).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 and described in the text and figure legend.

claim: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice in Eco-HAB.
source: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in either of the tested groups: (a) control (n = 23) or (b) valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice (n = 26), (c) control (n = 32) or (d) valproate-treated BALB/c mice (n = 19).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 and described in the text and figure legend.

claim: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in control BALB/c mice in Eco-HAB.
source: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in either of the tested groups: (a) control (n = 23) or (b) valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice (n = 26), (c) control (n = 32) or (d) valproate-treated BALB/c mice (n = 19).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 and described in the text and figure legend.

claim: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in valproate-treated BALB/c mice in Eco-HAB.
source: Social hierarchy does not correlate with exploration of the territory in either of the tested groups: (a) control (n = 23) or (b) valproate-treated C57BL/6 mice (n = 26), (c) control (n = 32) or (d) valproate-treated BALB/c mice (n = 19).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 and described in the text and figure legend.

claim: The testing environment in Eco-HAB is spacious, resembles the natural habitat of mice, and exploits innate behavioral patterns of this species to test relevant aspects of mouse sociability.
source: The testing environment is spacious, resembles the natural habitat of mice, and exploits innate behavioral patterns of this species to test relevant aspects of mouse sociability.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the system's design principles.

claim: Unlike short-term assessment using manual tests, Eco-HAB allows for long-term monitoring of social behaviors.
source: Unlike short-term assessment using manual tests, Eco-HAB allows for long-term monitoring of social behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the system.

claim: Individual tracking with RFID technology allows testing of group-housed animals without human handling – the most important confounding factor in manually conducted tests.
source: Individual tracking with RFID technology allows testing of group-housed animals without human handling – the most important confounding factor in manually conducted tests.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of the RFID-based approach.
